title: Cloud Networking Primitives
summary: How a cloud provider's virtual network is built and secured — the provider-specific layer on top of general TCP/IP networking.

slides.markdown:
A cloud network is a **software-defined** re-creation of everything a physical data center network does — subnets, routing, firewalls — except it's all API calls and config, not cables and switches.

The core idea: you get a private, isolated slice of the cloud (a **VPC**), you carve it into **subnets**, and you control exactly what can reach what with layered filtering rules.

slides.subTitle: Your private slice of the cloud
slides.markdown:
A **VPC** (Virtual Private Cloud) is an isolated network you define within the provider's infrastructure — your own private IP address range that nothing outside it can see by default. Within a VPC, you carve out **subnets**: smaller IP ranges, each tied to one Availability Zone, that group resources by role or exposure level.

A typical design: one subnet per AZ per tier — a web subnet and a database subnet, each duplicated across two or three AZs for resilience.

slides.subTitle: Why NAT gateways exist
slides.markdown:
A **public subnet** has a route to an internet gateway, so its resources can be reached from (and reach) the internet directly. A **private subnet** has no such route — nothing inbound from the internet can reach it directly, which is exactly where you put databases and internal services.

But private-subnet resources often still need *outbound* access — to fetch OS updates or call a third-party API. A **NAT gateway**, sitting in a public subnet, lets private resources initiate outbound connections while still blocking any unsolicited inbound connection from reaching them.

slides.subTitle: Stateful vs stateless filtering
slides.markdown:
| | Security groups | Network ACLs |
|---|---|---|
| Attached to | Individual resources (e.g. a VM) | A whole subnet |
| State | Stateful — a reply to an allowed request is auto-allowed | Stateless — you must explicitly allow both directions |
| Rules | Allow-only | Allow and deny |

**How to decide:** security groups are your primary, fine-grained tool for per-resource rules; network ACLs are a coarser, subnet-wide backstop — useful for an explicit deny (e.g. blocking a known-bad IP range) that a security group alone can't express.

Following one request shows every hop a packet makes and where it can be filtered or blocked.

![Packet path through a VPC with public/private subnets and a NAT gateway](assets/vpc-packet-path.svg)

Inbound traffic enters via the internet gateway into the public subnet; the private-subnet app never faces the internet directly. An outbound call from that app routes through the NAT gateway, masking its private IP before the request leaves the VPC.

slides.subTitle: L4 vs L7, internal vs internet-facing
slides.markdown:
A **Layer 4 (L4)** load balancer distributes raw TCP/UDP connections without looking at the content — fast, protocol-agnostic. A **Layer 7 (L7)** load balancer understands HTTP itself, so it can route by path or header, terminate TLS, and do content-based routing.

A load balancer is also either **internet-facing** (has a public IP, fronts your internet-facing service) or **internal** (only reachable from inside the VPC — the typical choice for routing traffic between your own app and internal services).

slides.subTitle: Connecting networks at scale
slides.markdown:
| | VPC peering | Transit gateway |
|---|---|---|
| Topology | Direct 1-to-1 link between two VPCs | Hub-and-spoke — one gateway, many VPCs attached |
| Scaling to N VPCs | O(N²) connections — gets unmanageable fast | O(N) — each VPC just attaches to the hub |
| Transitive routing | No — peering doesn't chain | Yes — any attached VPC can reach any other |

**How to decide:** peering is fine for two or three VPCs; once you're connecting a handful of teams' VPCs together, a transit gateway avoids the connection explosion and gives you central routing control.

slides.subTitle: Locking down a database subnet
slides.markdown:
To lock down a database from the internet: place it in a private subnet with no route to an internet gateway, attach a security group that allows inbound only from the app tier's security group on the database port (not from any IP range), and rely on the NAT gateway only if the database itself needs outbound access (e.g. for patching) — otherwise skip NAT entirely.

The result: even if someone finds the database's private IP, there's no network path from the public internet to reach it at all.

**Wrong belief:** "I'll open port range 0-65535 to 0.0.0.0/0 temporarily to debug, then lock it down later."

**Why it's wrong:** "temporarily" security-group rules are one of the most common real-world breach causes — automated scanners find open ports within minutes, and "later" often never comes because nothing visibly breaks in the meantime.

**Correct model:** open only the specific port you need, only to the specific source (an IP range or another security group) that needs it, and treat any 0.0.0.0/0 rule on a non-public-facing port as a standing incident.

slides.subTitle: Designing the network for a 3-tier app
slides.markdown:
When asked to design the network for a 3-tier app, walk through it tier by tier: a public subnet for the load balancer, a private subnet for the app tier reachable only from the load balancer's security group, and a private subnet for the database reachable only from the app tier's security group — each duplicated across two or more AZs.

Name the NAT gateway explicitly for any outbound need from the private tiers, and close by naming what a network ACL would add as a coarser backstop. That layer-by-layer walkthrough is what separates a real answer from a list of buzzwords.
